impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patent claims covering humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy written-description and enablement requirements under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating a jury verdict that Lilly willfully infringed Teva's patents covering methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache. The patents cover the active ingredient in Teva's Ajovy product, a competitor to Lilly's migraine treatments. This decision has major implications for the scope of patent protection available for biologic antibody therapies.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces that patent holders in the biologics space can obtain broad genus claims covering humanized antibodies where the specification discloses known methods of making such antibodies, even if only one specific antibody is exemplified. Strengthens patent protection for pharmaceutical innovators.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors developing biosimilar or alternative antibody therapies face heightened infringement risk from broadly drafted biologic patent claims. The willful infringement finding could expose Lilly to enhanced damages on remand.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions using an emulator and a model of function calls are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether damages may be based on foreign sales of infringing software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict, holding that Columbia's cybersecurity patent claims were directed to an abstract idea at Alice step one and remanding for further analysis at step two. The court also ruled that damages based on Norton's foreign sales were improper. The decision also vacated enhanced damages and attorneys' fees that relied in part on an improper contempt finding against Norton's counsel.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides technology companies with stronger defenses against patent infringement claims based on software security patents. Limits extraterritorial patent damages, protecting companies with global software distribution from inflated U.S. damages awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Universities and patent holders with cybersecurity and software-method patents face increased vulnerability to Alice § 101 challenges. Narrows the ability to recover damages based on worldwide sales of infringing software products.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet filed suit alleging misappropriation of trade secrets relating to its Omnipod insulin patch pump.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict finding trade secret misappropriation, holding that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred. Despite evidence that former Insulet employees shared CAD files and proprietary manufacturing information with competitor EOFlow, the court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit. The decision vacated the damages award and permanent injunction.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides companies accused of trade secret misappropriation with a strong statute of limitations defense where the trade secret owner had early knowledge of the alleged theft. Reinforces that companies must act promptly upon discovering potential misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face significant risk of losing claims if they delay filing suit after discovering potential misappropriation. Companies must implement robust monitoring and prompt legal action protocols when employees depart for competitors.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the plaintiff presented legally sufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether the same ideas could constitute inventive contributions for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed jury findings of trade secret misappropriation, holding that the plaintiff failed to show the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known in the field. The court vacated the reasonable royalty, exemplary damages, and permanent injunction. It also reversed a patent invalidity finding, holding that the same generally known ideas could not constitute inventive contributions for inventorship purposes. The counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides companies with stronger defenses against trade secret claims where the alleged secrets consist of information that is generally known in the relevant field. Clarifies the evidentiary threshold for establishing trade secret protectability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must clearly demonstrate that asserted secrets provide value beyond what is generally known in the industry. Bare assertions of secrecy without proof of novelty or independent economic value may be insufficient to sustain a claim.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement of a multicore processor patent based on extraterritoriality and by striking damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure in damages contentions.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding Intel's domestic acts of infringement. The court affirmed the rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory but reversed the striking of certain damages expert theories, finding the discovery sanctions were disproportionate. The case was remanded for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the court's rejection of overly broad extraterritoriality defenses where domestic acts of infringement can be shown. The reversal of the damages expert exclusion provides more flexibility in presenting damages theories.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global manufacturing and design processes face continued infringement exposure for activities with sufficient domestic nexus. Companies cannot rely solely on the location of chip design or manufacture to avoid U.S. patent liability.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of two patents relating to non-uniform constellations used in digital broadcast communication, while affirming eligibility for claims of two other patents. The court affirmed the denial of LG's motions for JMOL on noninfringement and damages. The decision provides important guidance on the line between abstract mathematical concepts and patent-eligible improvements to communication technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technical implementations of mathematical optimization in communications systems may retain eligibility for certain claim formulations. Affirming damages and infringement findings preserves significant monetary awards for patent owners.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing industry-standard communication technologies face continued patent infringement risk. The partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty about the scope of protection for patents rooted in mathematical optimization of signal constellations.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent owners who have granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue for infringement and other exclusionary rights have constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who grant an exclusive license but retain meaningful exclusionary rights—including the right to sue for infringement, approval rights over sublicenses and assignments, and retained rights to make and sell products—have Article III standing to sue infringers. The court emphasized that the retained right to sue was not rendered illusory by the license terms.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners can structure exclusive licenses while retaining litigation rights and still maintain standing to enforce patents against infringers. Provides clarity for licensing arrangements where patentees wish to monetize rights while preserving enforcement ability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face a broader range of potential plaintiffs, as patent owners with retained exclusionary rights can sue independently of their licensees. Challenges to standing based on the existence of exclusive licenses become more difficult.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) deposition testimony from a corporate representative who lacked personal knowledge of pre-critical-date product sales was admissible to prove the on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity, holding that a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge at summary judgment, and that computer source code consisting of machine commands is not hearsay. The court upheld the on-sale bar invalidation of engine-controller reprogramming patents based on prior sales of a competing product more than one year before the priority date.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides accused infringers with powerful evidentiary tools for invalidity defenses: 30(b)(6) witnesses need not have personal knowledge, and source code is admissible as non-hearsay. Strengthens on-sale bar challenges where the prior art company has undergone personnel changes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges supported by corporate testimony from representatives who were not employed at the time of the alleged prior art sales. The broad admissibility of source code as non-hearsay may make it easier to prove anticipation.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a temperature standard in the field, and whether the patent holder was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no literal infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents, agreeing that pH values in the claims should be measured at the standard temperature recognized in the field (25°C). The court also upheld the finding that Actelion was barred from asserting and had not proved infringement by equivalents, allowing Mylan to proceed with its generic drug application.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers benefit from the clarity that pH-based claims will be construed using field-standard measurement conditions, facilitating design-around strategies for ANDA filers. Strengthens the ability to bring generic alternatives to market.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical innovators with claims defined by pH or similar environment-dependent parameters face narrower claim scope, as courts will apply industry-standard measurement conditions rather than broader interpretations.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement functionality violated Section 337 by infringing Masimo's patents on user-worn physiological measurement devices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing and selling Apple Watch models that infringed Masimo's blood oximetry patents, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing Apple Watches. The court found no error in the Commission's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces the ITC as a powerful enforcement forum for patent holders against major technology companies, particularly for wearable health technology patents. Validates that smaller innovators can successfully use Section 337 to exclude products of much larger competitors.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies integrating health-monitoring features into consumer devices face significant exclusion-order risk at the ITC. Apple faces continued inability to import Apple Watch models with blood oxygen functionality, potentially affecting product strategy and revenue.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay of a refiled declaratory judgment action under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) after having missed the deadline to seek a stay of its original declaratory judgment action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the mandatory stay deadline under § 1659(a) by dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action after the statutory deadline has passed. The court prevented BioMarin from obtaining a mandatory stay of Ascendis's declaratory judgment action challenging patent infringement allegations related to competing achondroplasia treatments, allowing the district court litigation to proceed concurrently with the ITC investigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Declaratory judgment plaintiffs can maintain parallel district court proceedings even when ITC investigations are pending, provided the opposing party missed the statutory stay deadline. Prevents strategic manipulation of the mandatory stay provision through voluntary dismissal and refiling tactics.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC complainants who miss the 30-day window to request a mandatory stay cannot later obtain one by refiling, reducing their ability to consolidate patent disputes exclusively at the ITC.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a patent damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy where the patent holder was denied the opportunity to supplement its expert analysis.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report in its patent infringement suit against Microsoft's Azure platform technology, finding that the district court applied too rigid a standard. The court vacated the summary judgment of no remedy and the denial of Exafer's motion to reopen discovery, remanding for further proceedings. The decision emphasizes that patent holders should not be denied their day in court based on curable deficiencies in damages methodology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders receive greater protection against premature dismissal of infringement cases based on damages expert exclusions, particularly when deficiencies may be curable. Encourages courts to allow supplementation rather than outright exclusion of damages theories.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers like Microsoft may face prolonged litigation even after successfully challenging damages expert reports, as courts must now consider whether deficiencies can be remedied before granting summary judgment.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in its obviousness determination regarding sensor-based logistics patent claims, particularly concerning claims requiring reporting sensor information after a predetermined time delay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's finding that all challenged claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent were unpatentable as obvious and remanded for further proceedings. The case also raised questions about Qualcomm filing IPR petitions on the filing deadline of a party involved in related district court litigation, though the court declined to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer scrutiny of obviousness determinations, particularly where dependent claims add specific technical limitations. May deter third parties from filing strategic IPR petitions timed to assist parties in related litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR as a defense strategy face uncertainty when obviousness findings are vacated on appeal, potentially prolonging both IPR and related district court proceedings.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund expenses unrelated to operating the PACER system, and whether incentive awards to class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the approval of a $125 million settlement in a nationwide class action challenging excessive PACER fees, finding the district court did not abuse its discretion. The court upheld attorneys' fees awards and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, rejecting an objector's arguments that the settlement was inadequate and that incentive awards violated Supreme Court precedent. Hundreds of thousands of PACER users will receive full or substantial reimbursement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Validates that nationwide class settlements involving government fee overcharges can be approved where the settlement provides meaningful recovery to class members. Supports the continued availability of incentive awards to class representatives in appropriate cases.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner may correct inventorship under 35 U.S.C. § 256(b) when it cannot locate a missing coinventor, and whether the patents are invalid for omitting a coinventor.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that patents naming only two of four coinventors were invalid for incorrect inventorship where the patent owner could not locate a missing coinventor to obtain consent for correction under § 256. The court held that judicial correction under § 256(b) was unavailable because the patent owner failed to demonstrate diligent efforts to locate the missing inventor. The decision effectively invalidated patents covering vertical cable railing panels.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides accused infringers with a potent invalidity defense when patents omit coinventors, particularly foreign contributors. Incentivizes companies to properly identify and document all contributors to inventions at the outset.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that collaborate with foreign manufacturers on product development face serious risk of patent invalidity if foreign contributors to the invention are not named as coinventors and later become unreachable. Highlights the critical importance of proper inventorship determination during patent prosecution.
